questions.q: Which approach is the only one that can prevent 100% of memory-safety vulnerabilities?
choices: Using a memory-safe language such as Rust, Go, or Java
Enabling stack canaries and ASLR together
Replacing unsafe C library calls with bounded versions
Running extensive fuzz testing before release
questions.explain: Memory-safe languages use compile-time and runtime checks to rule out memory errors entirely. Mitigations, safe libraries and testing all reduce risk but can't guarantee you'll catch every bug.

questions.q: C has one real advantage over a garbage-collected language like Go: more deterministic memory allocation. Why doesn't that argument hold against Rust?
choices: Rust is memory-safe and not garbage-collected, so it is also deterministic
Rust compiles to C before it is executed
Rust disables ASLR, so its allocations are predictable
Rust's garbage collector runs at fixed, scheduled intervals
questions.explain: Rust gets memory safety without garbage collection, so C doesn't even keep its determinism advantage.

questions.q: Which bounds-checked C library function should replace gets?
questions.explain: fgets takes a maximum length, so it can't read past the end of the destination buffer.

questions.q: Which functions are safer replacements for strcpy?
choices: strncpy
strlcpy
sprintf
gets
questions.explain: strncpy and strlcpy take a length bound. sprintf (replace with snprintf) and gets (replace with fgets) are unsafe themselves.

questions.q: Which bounds-checked C library function should replace sprintf?
questions.explain: snprintf takes the size of the destination buffer and won't write past it.

questions.q: What does fuzz testing do?
choices: Feeds the program random inputs to try to trigger crashes or bugs
Checks every pointer for null before it is dereferenced
Reports memory leaks after the program exits
Measures which lines of code the test suite has executed
questions.explain: Fuzzing throws random inputs at the program. Leak detection is Valgrind's job, and code-coverage tools measure how much of the code the tests executed.

questions.q: Which practice is defensive programming?
choices: Null-checking a pointer before dereferencing it, even when you're sure it's valid
Randomizing the base address of the stack on every run
Placing a random value between local variables and the saved return address
Paying an outside firm to review the code
questions.explain: Defensive programming means always adding checks, even ones that seem unnecessary. It relies on programmer discipline and is tedious.

questions.q: True or false: Exploit mitigations such as stack canaries fix the underlying memory-safety bug.
questions.explain: They're mitigations, not fixes. The bug is still there, but exploiting it becomes harder or crashes the program, and mitigations aren't foolproof.

questions.q: Why is it worth combining several mitigations instead of relying on just one?
choices: Each can be bypassed alone, but together they force the attacker to find multiple vulnerabilities
Each mitigation only works if the others are also enabled
Combining them turns C into a memory-safe language
Compilers refuse to enable any single mitigation by itself
questions.explain: Defense in depth: layers work together. Bypassing several mitigations at once usually takes several separate bugs.

questions.q: What rule do non-executable pages enforce?
choices: Each page of memory can be writable or executable, but never both
No page of memory can ever be written after the program starts
Only the stack may be executed
Library code is writable but not executable
questions.explain: W^X (Write XOR Execute): a page is writable or executable, never both, so eip/rip can never point into memory the attacker could write.

questions.q: Which names refer to the non-executable pages defense?
choices: W^X
DEP
NX bit
ASLR
PAC
questions.explain: W^X (Write XOR Execute), DEP (Data Execution Prevention) and the NX bit are all names for the same idea. ASLR and PAC are separate mitigations.

questions.q: An attacker overflows a buffer with [shellcode] + [4 bytes garbage] + [&buf]. Which mitigation directly prevents the shellcode from running?
choices: Non-executable pages
Pointer authentication with a leaked key
Safe library functions
Valgrind
questions.explain: The shellcode sits in buf on the stack, which is writable and therefore not executable. Jumping to &buf crashes instead of running it.

questions.q: True or false: Non-executable pages stop return-to-libc attacks.
questions.explain: Return-to-libc jumps to existing library code, which is legitimately executable. The arguments it uses are data, not code, so NX doesn't block them.

questions.q: In a 32-bit x86 return-to-libc attack that calls execv, how does the attacker supply the function's argument (e.g., a filename string)?
choices: Places it on the stack where the function expects its arguments
Loads it into a register by injecting a mov instruction
Writes it into the libc code section
Passes it through an environment variable that libc re-executes
questions.explain: x86 passes arguments on the stack, so the attacker writes the argument at the right offset during the overflow. It's data, so NX doesn't stop it.

questions.q: In return-oriented programming (ROP), what is a gadget?
choices: A short instruction sequence already in memory that usually ends in ret
A complete library function with its own prologue and epilogue
A piece of injected shellcode stored on the heap
A compiler-inserted check that validates return addresses
questions.explain: Gadgets are snippets of existing code ending in ret. They don't need to be whole functions, so they need no prologue or epilogue.

questions.q: In a ROP chain, how does execution move from one gadget to the next?
choices: The ret at the end of each gadget pops the next address the attacker placed on the stack
Each gadget contains a hard-coded jmp to the next gadget
The CPU follows a table of gadget addresses stored in the code section
The attacker's shellcode calls each gadget as a function
questions.explain: The attacker overwrites a chain of return addresses starting at rip. Each ret pops the next address and jumps there.

questions.q: What can ROP do that basic return-to-libc can't?
choices: Perform arbitrary computation by stitching together existing code
Execute code on pages that are writable
Bypass the need to overwrite rip
Run without any existing code in memory
questions.explain: Return-to-libc calls one existing function. ROP chains gadgets into custom shellcode built from existing code, so it can do arbitrary computation.

questions.q: An attacker emulates add $0x4, %edx with two gadgets: (1) mov %edx,%eax; leave; ret and (2) add $0x4,%eax; pop %ebx; leave; ret. Which side effects does the attacker have to account for?
choices: The result ends up in EAX rather than EDX
EBX is clobbered by the pop
EDX is set to zero
ECX is incremented by 4
questions.explain: Gadget 1 copies EDX into EAX and gadget 2 adds 4 to EAX, so the result is in EAX. pop %ebx overwrites EBX. EDX and ECX aren't modified.

questions.q: True or false: A large enough codebase usually contains enough gadgets to build any shellcode, and ROP compilers can generate the chain automatically.
questions.explain: That's why NX alone is a weak barrier today. ROP compilers take a binary and the desired behavior and output a gadget chain.

questions.q: Where is a stack canary placed?
choices: Above the local variables and below the saved sfp/rip
Below the local variables, at the lowest address in the frame
Above the saved rip, in the caller's frame
In the unused high bits of the return address
questions.explain: Overflows usually write consecutive, increasing addresses, so a buffer overflow has to pass the canary before it reaches sfp/rip.

questions.q: When is the stack canary checked?
choices: Just before the function returns
Every time a local variable is written
When the function is first called
Only when the program exits
questions.explain: The function never uses the canary. It's checked right before returning, and the program crashes if it changed.

questions.q: True or false: A stack canary is fixed at compile time and stays the same every time the program runs.
questions.explain: Canaries are generated at runtime and change on every run. Otherwise the attacker could record the value once and reuse it.

questions.q: True or false: Within a single run of a program, the canary value is usually the same for every function.
questions.explain: One random value is typically chosen per run and used by every function.

questions.q: Why do real stack canaries usually contain a null byte?
choices: String functions like strcpy stop copying at a null byte, so they can't write the canary's correct value past it
A null byte makes the canary easier to check quickly
The CPU needs a null byte to tell the canary apart from a return address
It increases the canary's entropy
questions.explain: An attacker using a string-copy overflow can't write a null byte and keep going. The cost is one byte of entropy.

questions.q: A 32-bit stack canary contains one null byte. How many bits of entropy does it have?
questions.explain: 32 bits minus 8 fixed bits for the null byte leaves 24 random bits, so each guess has a 1 in 2^24 chance.

questions.q: A 64-bit stack canary contains one null byte. How many bits of entropy does it have?
questions.explain: 64 - 8 = 56 bits. At 1000 guesses per second, that's over 2 million years on average.

questions.q: Which attacks can still succeed against a program protected only by stack canaries?
choices: A heap overflow that corrupts heap data
Overflowing a buffer to change an adjacent local variable like an authenticated flag
A format string bug that writes directly to rip without touching the canary
A consecutive stack overflow from a buffer up through the saved rip
questions.explain: Canaries only catch consecutive writes that pass through them on the stack. Heap attacks, overwrites of other locals that stop before the canary, and non-consecutive writes all get past them.

questions.q: An attacker uses a format string bug to leak the canary. What must be true for this to help the overflow succeed?
choices: The overflow has to write the leaked value back in the same run of the program
The leaked value can be reused in any later run
The attacker must also leak the canary of every other function
The canary must not contain a null byte
questions.explain: The canary changes every run, so a leaked value only works in the run it came from.

questions.q: A 32-bit service restarts after each crash, so an attacker can keep guessing the canary. What makes this brute-force attack infeasible?
choices: Adding an exponentially increasing delay after each crash
Placing the canary below the local variables
Making the canary the same in every run
Removing the null byte from the canary
questions.explain: At thousands of tries per second, 2^24 guesses take a few hours. Exponential backoff after crashes makes that number of tries impractical.

questions.q: Where does pointer authentication store the pointer authentication code (PAC)?
choices: In the unused high bits of a 64-bit address
In a separate word right above the saved rip
In a dedicated region of the heap
In the lowest byte of the address, replacing the null byte
questions.explain: 64-bit address spaces don't use all 64 bits, so the top bits are always 0. The PAC goes there.

questions.q: A system has a 4 TB address space, which needs 42 bits. How many high bits of a 64-bit pointer are always 0 and free to hold a PAC?
questions.explain: 64 - 42 = 22 unused high bits.

questions.q: In a 40-bit address space, rip = 0x0000001234567899 and its PAC is 0xABCDEF. What 64-bit value is stored on the stack? (Write it in hex with a 0x prefix.)
questions.explain: The 24-bit PAC fills the unused top 24 bits: 0xABCDEF followed by the 40-bit address 1234567899.

questions.q: With per-pointer PAC, the code is computed as PAC = f(KEY, ADDRESS). What kind of function is f?
choices: A MAC: deterministic, and you can't produce valid outputs without the key
A random number generator that gives a new PAC each time it's called
A simple checksum of the address bits that anyone can compute
A public-key encryption of the address
questions.explain: f is deterministic, so the CPU stores only the key and recomputes the PAC on every check. Without the key, nobody can forge valid PACs.

questions.q: True or false: If an attacker leaks a valid pointer and its PAC, they can attach that PAC to a different address of their choice and pass the check.
questions.explain: The PAC depends on the address, so f(KEY, new address) won't match the old PAC. Leaked pairs don't help with a new address.

questions.q: What happens if code dereferences a pointer that still has its PAC in the high bits, without going through the CPU's check?
choices: The program crashes, because the high bits make it an invalid address
The CPU silently ignores the high bits
The PAC is verified automatically and stripped
It reads from a random location in the heap
questions.explain: Only the authentication check restores the original zero bits. With the PAC still in them, the address is invalid.

questions.q: Which are realistic ways to subvert pointer authentication?
choices: Guess the PAC (e.g., 1 in 2^20 for a 20-bit PAC)
Use another bug to trick the program into creating a validated pointer
Steal the key from the CPU or break f
Reuse a leaked PAC with a different address
questions.explain: Guessing, getting the program to sign a pointer for you, and stealing the key or breaking f all work. A leaked PAC is tied to its own address.

questions.q: An attacker uses a format string bug to write directly to rip, skipping the stack canary. Which mitigation still catches this?
choices: Pointer authentication
Non-executable pages
A larger stack canary
Safe library functions
questions.explain: PAC protects the pointer itself, so changing rip without producing a matching PAC fails the check, no matter how the write happened.

questions.q: What does ASLR randomize on each run?
choices: The start address of each memory section (stack, heap, code, static data, each library)
The order of local variables within each stack frame
The offset between the saved sfp and rip
The instructions inside each function
questions.explain: ASLR moves whole sections, so absolute addresses change but layout within a section doesn't.

questions.q: True or false: ASLR randomizes relative offsets, such as the distance between the saved sfp and rip.
questions.explain: Only section start addresses are randomized. Relative offsets stay fixed, so one leaked address reveals the addresses of nearby data.

questions.q: What limits the amount of randomness ASLR can provide?
choices: Sections have to start on a page boundary
The random number generator is only 8 bits
The stack must always start at the same address
Libraries can't be relocated
questions.explain: Section starts have to be multiples of the page size (typically 4096 bytes on 32-bit), which removes the low bits from the randomness.

questions.q: About how many bits of entropy might ASLR provide on a 32-bit system?
questions.explain: Roughly 16 bits, a 1 in 2^16 chance per guess. At one guess per second, that's under a day.

questions.q: Why does ASLR have low overhead?
choices: Libraries are already dynamically linked at runtime, so segments are relocatable anyway
The CPU randomizes addresses in hardware at no cost
ASLR only runs once, when the program is compiled
ASLR only randomizes the stack
questions.explain: Dynamic linking already requires relocatable code, so placing segments at random addresses costs little extra.

questions.q: A format string bug leaks one saved sfp. Why does that help the attacker against ASLR?
choices: Relative offsets are fixed, so the attacker can work out the addresses of nearby data like rip
It permanently turns ASLR off for the process
It reveals the random seed for every later run
It lets the attacker execute code on the stack
questions.explain: Since layout within the section doesn't change, the attacker can compute nearby addresses from one leaked one (e.g., rip is 4 bytes above sfp on 32-bit).

questions.q: Against ASLR + NX, how does each mitigation contribute?
choices: NX blocks injected shellcode, and ASLR hides the addresses of existing code needed for ROP or return-to-libc
ASLR blocks injected shellcode, and NX hides code addresses
Both only protect the heap
NX detects overwritten return addresses, and ASLR encrypts pointers
questions.explain: Without NX, the attacker could inject code. Without ASLR, they would know where existing code is for ROP or ret2libc.

questions.q: To exploit a program protected by both ASLR and NX, what does the attacker typically need?
choices: A memory leak that reveals addresses
A memory write that places a ROP chain
Only a single stack buffer overflow with injected shellcode
Physical access to the machine
questions.explain: The leak defeats ASLR and the write defeats NX, so the attacker needs two vulnerabilities.

questions.q: Which mitigation is aimed at stopping an attacker who hard-codes absolute addresses into an exploit?
choices: ASLR
Stack canaries
Non-executable pages
fgets instead of gets
questions.explain: ASLR changes absolute addresses on every run, so hard-coded addresses for shellcode, libc functions or gadgets stop working.
